Tischler and Piet Maes The citation for this ICTV Report chapter is the summary published as: Bradfute, S. B., Calisher, C. H., Klempa, B., Klingström, J., Kuhn, J. H., Laenen, L., Tischler, N. D., & Maes, P. (2024). ICTV Virus Taxonomy Profile: Hantaviridae 2024, Journal of General Virology 105, 001975 Corresponding author: Piet Maes ( [email protected] ) Edited by: Holly Hughes and Evelien Adriaenssens Posted: March 2024, updated June 2024 Summary Hantaviridae is a family for negative-sense RNA viruses with genomes of about 10.5–14.6 kb (Table 1 Hantaviridae ). The family includes eight genera ( Actinovirus and Percilovirus (subfamily Actantavirinae ), Agnathovirus (subfamily Agantavirinae ), Loanvirus , Mobatvirus , Orthohantavirus and Thottimvirus (subfamily Mammantavirinae ), and Reptillovirus (subfamily Repantavirinae ). These viruses are maintained in and/or transmitted by small mammals, but also by fish and reptiles. Several orthohantaviruses can infect humans, causing mild, severe, and sometimes-fatal diseases. Hantavirids produce enveloped virions containing three single-stranded RNA segments with open reading frames (ORFs) that encode a nucleoprotein (N), a glycoprotein precursor (GPC), and large (L) protein containing an RNA-directed RNA polymerase (RdRP) domain. Table 1 Hantaviridae. Characteristics of members of the family Hantaviridae. Characteristic Description* Example Hantaan virus (S segment: M14626; M segment: M14627; L segment: X55901), species Orthohantavirus hantanense Virion Enveloped, pleomorphic virions 80–160 nm in diameter with heterodimeric surface spikes Genome Three single-stranded RNA molecules (segments): small (S; 1.0–3.0 kb), medium (M; 3.4–4.8 kb), and large (L; 5.3–6.8 kb) Replication Ribonucleoprotein (RNP) complexes containing anti-genomic RNA serve as coding templates for synthesis of genomic RNA Translation Proteins are produced from capped and non-polyadenylated mRNAs. The 5′-cap structure is obtained via cap-snatching from cellular mRNAs Host range Fish (actinoviruses, agnathoviruses, perciloviruses), mammals (orthohantaviruses), and reptiles (reptilloviruses) Taxonomy Realm Riboviria , kingdom Orthornavirae , phylum Negarnaviricota , class Bunyaviricetes , order Elliovirales ; the family includes four subfamilies, eight genera, and 55 species * mostly based on experiments with mammalian orthohantaviruses Viruses assigned to each of the seven genera form genus-specifc monophyletic clades based on phylogenetic analysis of concatenated L protein/RdRP, glycoprotein and N sequences. Viruses from all seven genera share one or more of the following characteristics: (i) enveloped pleomorphic virions; (ii) tri-segmented, negative-sense RNA genome without polyadenylated tracts at the 3′-end; (iii) genomic sequence complementarity at the 5′- and 3′-ends; and (iv) capped but not polyadenylated virus mRNAs ( Maes et al., 2004 ). Piscine Hosts Genus Actinovirus . Viruses in this genus infect actinopterygian (percid, ogcocephalid, and triacanthodid, and possibly goblid and melanotaeniid) fish. Genus Agnathovirus . Viruses in this genus infect agnathan (myxinid) fish. Genus Percilovirus . Viruses in this genus infect actinopterygian ( gobiid, lophiid ) fish. Mammalian Hosts Genus Loanvirus. Viruses in this genus infect rhinolophid, verspertillionid, and possibly nycterid bats and possibly murid rodents. Genus Mobatvirus. Viruses in this genus infect emballonurid, hipposiderid, pteropodid and possibly molossid, and vespertillionid bats and soricid and talpid eulipotyphla. Genus Orthohantavirus. Viruses assigned to this genus infect soricid and talpid eulipotyphla and muroid and possibly dipodoid rodents. Genus Thottimvirus. Viruses in this genus infect soricid and possibly talpid eulipotyphla. Reptilian Hosts Genus Reptillovirus . Viruses in this genus infect gekkonid and possibly scincid reptiles. Virion Morphology Only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Physicochemical and physical properties Only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Nucleic acid Hantavirids have tri-segmented, negative-sense RNA genomes (S, M, and L segments). The viral mRNAs are not polyadenylated and contain a 5′-methylated cap and several non-templated nucleotides at the 5′-end that are derived from host cell mRNAs via cap snatching ( Schmaljohn et al., 1985 , Jonsson and Schmaljohn 2001 , Vaheri et al., 2013 ). Further information is only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Proteins Hantavirids typically express three structural proteins. The most abundant structural protein in a hantavirion is N, which encapsidates the hantaviral genomic segments. The least abundant protein is L, which mediates viral genome replication and transcription. Two glycoprotein subunits, G N and G C , are produced from GPC and mediate entry of hantavirions ( Schmaljohn et al., 1985 , Spiropoulou 2001 , Vaheri et al., 2013 ). Specifics are only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Lipids Not reported but are likely derived from the Golgi apparatus and/or the host cell plasma membrane and therefore likely composed of phospholipids, glycolipids, fatty acids, and sterols. Carbohydrates Only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Genome organization and replication S RNA encodes N and in some viruses NSs ( Jääskeläinen et al., 2007 , Vera-Otarola et al., 2012 ), M RNA encodes GPC, and the L RNA encodes L with its RdRP, helicase, and endonuclease domains ( Jonsson and Schmaljohn 2001 ) (Figure 1 Hantaviridae ). Specifics are only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Figure 1 Hantaviridae . Genome organization of representative hantaviruses. The 5′- and 3′- ends of all segments are complementary at their termini, likely promoting the formation of panhandle RNP complexes within the virion . GPC , glycoprotein precursor gene; L , large (protein) gene; N , nucleoprotein gene. Biology Hantavirids have been found in actinopterygian (gobiid, lophiid, percid, ogcocephalid, and triacanthodid, and possibly goblid and melanotaeniid) and agnathan (myxinid) fish; in emballonurid, hipposiderid, pteropodid, rhinolophid, verspertillionid, and possibly molossid and nycterid bats; in soricid and talpid eulipotyphla; in muroid and possibly dipodoid rodents; in gekkonid and possibly scincid reptiles; and potentially in coleopteran and plectopteran insects (see genus pages for details). Only orthohantaviruses are known to cause diseases (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Antigenicity Systematic antigenicity studies have only been reported for orthohantaviruses (see Orthohantavirus genus page). species demarcation criteria The availability of at least coding-complete sequences of all three genome segments may be sufficient for hantavirid classification in the absence of a cultured isolate. Demarcation of genera is based upon DivErsity pArtitioning by hieRarchical Clustering (DEmARC) analysis) using concatenated deduced S, M, and L segment expression product sequences ( Hantaviridae: current classification and future perspectives, Viruses, 11, 9, e0788">Laenen et al., 2019 ). DEmARC analysis gave a frequency distribution of Pairwise Evolutionary Distance (PED) values of which the threshold of 0.1 gave an optimal clustering cost of zero and is used as the hantavirid species demarcation criterium. Genera are demarked by a PED-value threshold of 0.95 and subfamilies are demarcated based on their distinct clustering in a Bayesian maximum clade credibility tree and a PED-value threshold of 3.5. Relationships within the family Phylogenetic relationships across the family have been estimated using Bayesian maximum clade credibility trees generated from complete N, GPC, and L amino-acid sequences; similar topologies are obtained with concatenated N and GPC sequences (Figure 2 Hantaviridae ). Figure 2 Hantaviridae . Maximum likelihood phylogenetic tree inferred using IQ-TREE. The tree was constructed based on 53 concatenated S and M segment (amino acid) sequences using the LG+R9 model of sequence evolution. Branch lengths represent the estimated number of substitutions per site. Bootstrap support values (>70%) are indicated at nodes, reflecting the degree of confidence in the branching pattern. Relationships with other taxa Hantavirids are closely related to bunyaviral crulivirids, fimovirids, peribunyavirids, phasmavirids, tulasvirids, and tospovirids ( Wolf et al., 2018 , Herath et al., 2020 ). Using the Master Species List Using the Virus Metadata Resource Using the Find the Species tool Using the ICTV Report Webinar Webinar on Virus Taxonomy Webinar on Finding Information GitHub Repository Zenodo Repository Email ICTV Help ‏‏‎ ‎ ICTV Report Book: Hantaviridae Family: Hantaviridae Subfamily: Actantavirinae Genus: Actinovirus Genus: Percilovirus Subfamily: Agantavirinae Genus: Agnathovirus Subfamily: Mammantavirinae Genus: Loanvirus Genus: Mobatvirus Genus: Orthohantavirus Genus: Thottimvirus Subfamily: Repantavirinae Genus: Reptillovirus Authors: Hantaviridae Citation: Hantaviridae References: Hantaviridae Resources: Hantaviridae Species List: Hantaviridae Subfamily: Mammantavirinae Genus: Orthohantavirus Distinguishing features Sixty different viruses are classified in the genus Orthohantavius. These viruses typically infect specific soricid and talpid eulipotyphla and muroid and possibly dipodoid rodents. Orthohantaviruses are the only hantavirids known to cause disease in humans ( Schmaljohn and Hjelle 1997 , Jonsson et al., 2010 , Kuhn and Schmaljohn 2023 , Vial et al., 2023 ). Virion Morphology Orthohantavirions are pleomorphic in shape, mostly spherical of 80–160 nm in diameter ( Huiskonen et al., 2010 ), and surrounded by a membrane envelope that is decorated with glycoprotein (GP) spikes composed of G N and G C subunits (Figure 1 Orthohantavirus ). The virion envelope is 5 nm thick and is decorated with square shaped spikes, consisting of tetrameric G N -G C heterodimers, which protrude 10 nM from the membrane forming a surface lattice of local symmetry interrupted by empty membrane spots ( Hung et al., 1983 , Huiskonen et al., 2010 , Battisti et al., 2011 , Parvate et al., 2019 , Serris et al., 2020 , Guardado-Calvo and Rey 2021 ). Isolated ribonucleoprotein (RNP) complexes are composed of individual segment genomic RNA encapsidated by nucleoprotein (N) ( Tao et al., 1987 , Huiskonen et al., 2010 , Battisti et al., 2011 , Hepojoki et al., 2012 , Guo et al., 2016 , Arragain et al., 2019 ). Virions assemble and bud from the Golgi complex or cell surface membranes, depending on the virus ( Goldsmith et al., 1995 , Parvate et al., 2019 ). Figure 1 Orthohantavirus. A, B) Electron micrographs of Tula virus particles adapted from ( Huiskonen et al., 2010 ). C) Schematic illustration of an orthohantavirus particle. Shown is a spherical and enveloped (grey) particle with glycoprotein spikes (G N yellow, G C blue) inserted in a bilaminar lipid envelope. The S (small), M (medium), and L (large) RNP (ribonucleoprotein) complexes inside the particle consist of N (nucleoprotein, green) and L (large protein, pink). ViralZone image reproduced courtesy of SwissBioPics. Physicochemical and physical properties Virion buoyant densities in sucrose and CsCl are 1.15–1.18 ( White et al., 1982 ) and 1.20–1.21 g cm −3 , respectively ( Schmaljohn et al., 1983 ). Virions are sensitive to chemical inactivation with, for instance, methanol, paraformaldehyde, acetone/methanol, N -ethylmaleimide or detergents, as well as physical methods such as heat, gamma irradiation or UV irradiation ( Kraus et al., 2005 , Strandin et al., 2011 , Elveborg et al., 2022 ). Nucleic acid Orthohantavirus genomes are linear tri-segmented RNA molecules of negative polarity. The genomes are about 11.1–12.3 kb in length (small [S] segment: 1.2–2.1 kb; medium [M] segment: 3.4–3.8 kb; large [L] segment: 6.5–6.6 kb). Proteins Orthohantaviruses typically express three structural proteins (Table 1 Orthohantavirus ). The most abundant structural protein in an orthohantavirion is N, which encapsidates the orthohantaviral genomic segments. The least abundant protein is L, which mediates viral genome replication and transcription. Two glycoprotein subunits, G N and G C , mediate virion entry. G N and G C and non-structural proteins are encoded as a precursor polyprotein. Table 1 Orthohantavirus . Location and function of orthohantavirus structural proteins. Protein Location, mass, and function Reference Nucleoprotein (N) Structural virion protein (about 48 kD). Oligomerizes and encapsidates orthohantaviral genomic segments and hence component of RNPs. Binds to L and G N ( Mir et al., 2010 , Reuter and Krüger 2018 , Arragain et al., 2019 ) Nonstructural protein (NSs) Non-structural protein encoded by some orhtohantaviruses. Has type I interferon inhibitory activity. May occur as multiple isoforms. ( Vera-Otarola et al., 2020 , Binder et al., 2021 ) Glycoprotein (GP) Structural virion protein consisting of two subunits (G N : about 70-75 kD, G C : about 50-55 kD). Produced via proteolytic cleavage from the genome-encoded precursor GPC. Projects from virion membranes as tetrameric GP spikes composed of G N and G C heterodimers. GP mediates cell- receptor binding; as a class II fusion machine it induces virion-cell membrane fusion and, thereby cell entry. G N binds to N and RNA ( Spiropoulou et al., 2003 , Tischler et al., 2005 , Cifuentes-Muñoz et al., 2014 , Li et al., 2016 , Willensky et al., 2016 , Rissanen et al., 2017 , Zhu et al., 2018 , Bignon et al., 2019 , Sperber et al., 2019 ) Large protein (L) Structural virion protein (246 kD) with RdRP, helicase, and endoribonuclease domains. Component of the RNP inside virions. Binds to N and RNA. Oligomerizes and mediates transcription and replication of viral RNA segments. Mediates cap-snatching for viral mRNA capping. ( Kukkonen et al., 2005 , Cheng et al., 2014 , Rothenberger et al., 2016 , Jeeva et al., 2019 , Durieux Trouilleton et al., 2023 ) Genome organization and replication The orthohantavirus genome consists of three negative-sense RNA molecules, termed S (small), M (medium), and L (large) (Figure 2 Orthohantavirus ). Figure 2 Orthohantavirus. Schematic representation of orthohantavirus genome organization. Orthohantavirus genomic segments assume circular forms via non-covalent binding of complementary and highly conserved 3′- and 5′-terminal sequences. Genomic segment reassortment mostly occurs among viruses belonging to the same species but interspecies reassortment likely occurs occasionally ( Klempa 2018 , Petazzi et al., 2021 ). Orthohantavirus infection starts with virion attachment, mediated by G N and G C , to cell-surface attachment factors and entry via the endosomal route ( Shtanko et al., 2014 ) (Figure 3 Orthohantavirus ). Figure 3 Orthohantavirus . Lifecycle of orthohantaviruses. (1) Virion attachment; (2) virion uptake; (3) virion-cell membrane fusion; (4) transcription; (5) translation; (6) replication; (7) virion assembly; and (8) virion egress. After engaging a cellular receptor, protocadherin 1 in the case of American orthohantaviruses, virion-membrane fusion results in early or late endosomal release, depending on the virus, of the virion RNP complex into the cytoplasm in a pH-dependent manner ( Jangra et al., 2018 , Mittler et al., 2019 , Torriani et al., 2019 , Dieterle et al., 2021 ). During primary transcription L generates uncapped antigenomic RNA molecules that are then capped using host cell-derived capped primers (cap snatching). L and S segment-transcribed mRNAs are translated by free ribosomes ( Garcin et al., 1995 , Jeeva et al., 2019 , Meier et al., 2021 ). M segment-transcribed mRNA is translated by membrane-bound ribosomes, with the expressed GPC which is likely co-translationally cleaved by cellular proteases to yield G N and G C . The synthesis of the antigenome by L protein serves as a template for genomic RNA replication. Secondary transcription amplifies the synthesis of mRNAs and genome replication. During morphogenesis, G N and G C accumulate in the Golgi apparatus, modified host membranes are acquired, and virions bud into the Golgi. Biology Genus Orthohantavirus includes 38 species for 60 distinct viruses. These viruses and their unclassified, potential relatives, subclinically, and often chronically, infect specific soricid and talpid eulipotyphla, and muroid and possibly dipodoid rodents ( Jonsson et al., 2010 , Wu et al., 2018 , Chen et al., 2023 , Kuhn and Schmaljohn 2023 ). Orthohantaviruses are overall distributed worldwide, but the individual geographic distribution is dependent on host range. At least some orthohantaviruses may not be as restricted to a particular host as originally thought, but may be carried by animals of multiple hosts ( Goodfellow et al., 2021 , Quizon et al., 2022 , Gu et al., 2023 ). Orthohantaviruses are the only hantavirids known to cause disease (all in humans) and all disease-causing viruses are rodent-borne. Human infection may occur after inhalation of aerosolized excreta or secreta of infected rodents or direct rodent contact. The two WHO-recognized orthohantavirus-caused diseases are hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), caused by Asian and European viruses (in particular Dobrava virus [DOBV], Hantaan virus [HTNV], Puumala virus [PUUV] and Seoul virus [SEOV]), and hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS), a frequently lethal disease caused by viruses from the Americas (in particular Andes virus [ANDV] and Sin Nombre virus [SNV]) ( Vial et al., 2023 ). The hamster model of wild-type ANDV infection is lethal and largely mimics human HPS ( Hooper et al., 2001 ). After SNV infection in nonhuman primates, some animals develop an HPS-like disease, but cell passage of SNV can result in mutations that render the virus non-pathogenic in this model ( Safronetz et al., 2014 ). Many rodent models result in a chronic, asymptomatic infection, and these have been used in early-stage therapeutic studies ( Strandin et al., 2020 ). However, recent advances have been made in development of an HFRS mouse model using HTNV variants ( Wei et al., 2022 ). Orthohantavirus animal models are reviewed in ( Golden et al., 2015 ). Antigenicity There is considerable serum cross-reactivity between the nucleocapsids of hantavirids, but neutralizing antibodies targeting Gn/Gc are more specific. SNV was first identified as a hantavirid based on cross-reactivity of patient sera with other orthohantavirus antigens ( 1993 ). Similarly, rodents that carried SNV were identified in serosurveys using non-SNV orthohantavirus antigens, since SNV had not been isolated at the time ( Childs et al., 1994 ). Species demarcation criteria Demarcation of species is based upon DivErsity pArtitioning by hieRarchical Clustering (DEmARC) analysis) using concatenated deduced S, M, and L segment expression product sequences ( Laenen et al., 2019 ). Phylogenetic relationships across the genus have been estimated using maximum likelihood trees generated from complete N, GPC and L amino-acid sequences, and for N and GPC amino-acid sequences (Figure 2 Hantaviridae ). Hantaviridae ~ ViralZone Skip to main content ViralZone Hantaviridae (taxid:1980413) VIRION Enveloped, spherical. Diameter from 80 to 120nm. GENOME Segmented Negative-stranded RNA linear genome, L segment is between 6.8 and 12 kb, M segment between 3.2 and 4.9 kb and S segment between 1 and 3 kb. Encodes for four to six proteins. Some hantaviruses also encode a NSs protein on their S segment. GENE EXPRESSION The viral RNA dependent RNA polymerase (L) binds to a promoter on each encapsidated segment, and transcribes the mRNA. These are capped by L protein during synthesis using cap snatching . Transcription is terminated by a strong hairpin sequence at the end of each gene. Puumala virus expressed an additional NSs by leaky scanning in the NS gene. ENZYMES RNA-dependent RNA polymerase L Cap Snatching endonuclease L REPLICATION CYTOPLASMIC Virus attaches to host receptors though Gn-Gc glycoprotein dimer, and is endocytosed into vesicles in the host cell. Fusion of virus membrane with the vesicle membrane; ribonucleocapsid segments are released in the cytoplasm. Transcription , viral mRNAs are capped in the cytoplasm. Replication presumably starts when enough nucleoprotein is present to encapsidate neo-synthetized antigenomes and genomes. The ribonucleocapsids buds at Golgi apparatus, releasing the virion by exocytosis. The hantaviruses (Hantaviridae) ~ ViralZone Skip to main content ViralZone Back to Andes virus resource There are approximately 92 known viruses in the family Hantaviridae, classified into 52 species. Each species is typically adapted to a specific reservoir host, most commonly rodents, but also bats and moles. With the notable exception of Andes virus, hantaviruses are generally not transmitted from person to person. Based on their geographic distribution, evolutionary relationships, and the diseases they cause in humans, hantaviruses can be broadly divided into three major groups: New World hantaviruses (the Americas) These viruses cause Hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS), a severe respiratory disease. Important examples include Sin Nombre virus and Andes virus. Annual incidence are about 100 cases per year (Andes virus) about 25 cases per year (Sin Nombre virus) Old World hantaviruses (Asia) These viruses are responsible for Hantavirus hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), which is characterized by fever, hemorrhage, and acute kidney injury. Major examples include Hantaan virus and Seoul virus. Annual incidence: more than 10,000 cases worldwide Old World hantaviruses (Europe) European hantaviruses typically cause a milder form of HFRS known as Nephropathia epidemica (NE). The main causative agents are Puumala virus and Dobrava-Belgrade virus. Annual incidence: more than 1,000 cases Together, these viruses represent an important and diverse group of zoonotic pathogens that can cause severe disease following accidental transmission from their natural animal hosts to humans.

papers.title: Ecological and Individual-Level Factors Associated With Hantavirus Cardiopulmonary Syndrome Notifications and in-Hospital Mortality Among Hospitalized Patients in Chile, 2005-2022.
papers.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS) is a severe zoonotic disease caused by Orthohantavirus andesense (Andes virus, ANDV), with significant public health burden in Chile. Despite decades of surveillance, knowledge gaps remain regarding the ecological drivers of notification burden and the individual-level determinants of in-hospital mortality among hospitalized patients. This study aimed to address both dimensions simultaneously, providing a multilevel characterization of HCPS epidemiology in Chile from 2005 to 2022. METHODS: Two complementary analyses were conducted. First, an ecological study examined district-level HCPS notifications (2005-2022) using a negative binomial mixed-effects model, with predictors including male population rate, urbanization proportion, population density, season and burned area due to forest fires during the most recent summer season. Second, an individual-level analysis of hospitalized HCPS patients (2010-2020) used a logistic mixed-effects model to identify correlates of in-hospital mortality among hospitalized patients, including age, sex, indigenous group affiliation, hospitalization duration and number of surgical interventions. RESULTS: A total of 886 HCPS cases were notified across 187 districts, averaging 49.2 cases per year. Notifications were positively associated with higher male population rates and greater burned area due to forest fires, and negatively associated with urbanization and population density. Among 462 hospitalized patients, the in-hospital case-fatality ratio was 19.7%. Older age, female sex and indigenous group affiliation were significantly associated with higher in-hospital mortality risk among hospitalized patients. Shorter hospitalization duration and greater number of surgical interventions, as correlates of clinical severity and complexity, were also associated with in-hospital mortality among hospitalized patients. CONCLUSIONS: HCPS notification burden in Chile is shaped by environmental and demographic factors, with forest fire activity representing a novel and actionable ecological risk indicator. In-hospital mortality among hospitalized patients is disproportionately concentrated in older, female, and indigenous populations, highlighting the need for targeted surveillance, equitable healthcare access and integrated One Health strategies to reduce the burden of HCPS in Chile.

Results: A total of 886 HCPS cases were notified across 187 districts, averaging 49.2 cases per year. Notifications were positively associated with higher male population rates and greater burned area due to forest fires, and negatively associated with urbanization and population density. Among 462 hospitalized patients, the in-hospital case-fatality ratio was 19.7%. Older age, female sex and indigenous group affiliation were significantly associated with higher in-hospital mortality risk among hospitalized patients. Shorter hospitalization duration and greater number of surgical interventions, as correlates of clinical severity and complexity, were also associated with in-hospital mortality among hospitalized patients. Conclusions: HCPS notification burden in Chile is shaped by environmental and demographic factors, with forest fire activity representing a novel and actionable ecological risk indicator. In-hospital mortality among hospitalized patients is disproportionately concentrated in older, female, and indigenous populations, highlighting the need for targeted surveillance, equitable healthcare access and integrated One Health strategies to reduce the burden of HCPS in Chile. papers.title: Hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome in children: a systematic scoping review of presentation, critical care management, and outcomes.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Pediatric hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome/hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HCPS/HPS) is rare but can progress rapidly from a nonspecific febrile prodrome to respiratory failure, shock, and multiorgan dysfunction. Pediatric-specific evidence is limited, and a comprehensive map of the clinical literature is lacking. METHODS: We conducted a systematic scoping review per Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR) guidance (protocol registered at DOI:10.17605/OSF.IO/MZDN4). PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science, and Cochrane CENTRAL were searched from inception to May 2026. Eligible reports described children or adolescents (age ≤18 years) with HCPS/HPS and extractable pediatric clinical data. Two reviewers independently screened records, assessed overlap, extracted data, and appraised reporting quality using Joanna Briggs Institute tools. RESULTS: Of 2208 database records, 20 reports were included in the core pediatric synthesis after removal of 976 duplicates and screening. Reports were concentrated in the Americas. Recurrent features included fever, gastrointestinal symptoms, myalgia, thrombocytopenia, hemoconcentration, pulmonary edema, respiratory failure, and shock. Severe cases required mechanical ventilation, vasoactive support, extracorporeal membrane oxygenation, and in some cases renal replacement therapy. Larger pediatric case series and surveillance-level reports reported mortality of approximately 33% to 37%. Evidence was predominantly case-based with variable reporting completeness. CONCLUSIONS: Pediatric HCPS/HPS is rare but potentially rapidly fatal. Early suspicion in endemic regions or after rodent exposure, with prompt supportive critical care and timely consideration of advanced cardiopulmonary support, is central to management.

analysis.background: Pediatric hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS/HPS) is rare but can progress rapidly from a nonspecific febrile prodrome to respiratory failure, shock, and multiorgan dysfunction (A1).
analysis.main_directions: The review maps the limited pediatric literature, describes common clinical features (fever, GI symptoms, myalgia, thrombocytopenia, pulmonary edema, shock) (A9), and outlines critical‑care interventions such as mechanical ventilation, vasoactive support, ECMO, and renal replacement therapy (A10).
analysis.current_state: Evidence is predominantly case‑based with variable completeness (A12); larger series report a mortality of roughly 33‑37% and most reports originate from the Americas (A11, A8).
analysis.gaps: Pediatric‑specific data are scarce, reporting is inconsistent, and the small number of studies limits robust conclusions about optimal management (A2, A12).
analysis.future_research: Prospective multicenter registries, standardized case reporting, and systematic evaluation of advanced cardiopulmonary support strategies are needed to improve early recognition and outcomes (A14).

analysis.summary_en: Background: Pediatric HCPS/HPS is rare but can rapidly become fatal (A1). Main directions: The scoping review catalogs clinical presentations and critical‑care measures such as ventilation, vasoactive drugs, ECMO, and renal therapy (A9‑A10). Current state: Data are mainly case reports with variable quality, mortality ~33‑37%, and reports concentrated in the Americas (A11, A12, A8). Gaps: Limited pediatric evidence and inconsistent reporting hinder definitive management guidance (A2, A12). Future research: Prospective registries, uniform reporting, and systematic assessment of advanced support are required (A14).

papers.title: Hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome: challenges faced by clinicians.

source_records.title: Hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome: challenges faced by clinicians.

papers.full_text: Managing hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS) in pediatric patients is highly challenging due to rapid clinical decline, diagnostic ambiguity, and the lack of targeted antiviral therapies. The article by Weerapong et al addresses these challenges in this issue of Baylor University Medical Center Proceedings.1 While the disease is rare in children, it carries a very high mortality rate of 30% to 50% if not managed aggressively. Because children possess unique physiological vulnerabilities, clinicians face several distinct obstacles when managing HCPS. Diagnostic dilemmas and misinterpretations stem from the nonspecific prodrome, which consists of flu-like symptoms including fever, headache, myalgia, and gastrointestinal issues such as vomiting or abdominal pain. These symptoms mirror common, benign childhood infections like influenza, gastroenteritis, or respiratory syncytial virus, thereby delaying clinical suspicion. Furthermore, obtaining a clear history of rodent exposure is difficult, as children may not notice or recall contact with deer mouse droppings while playing outdoors. Crucially, the shift from a benign viral prodrome to severe respiratory failure and cardiogenic shock occurs abruptly, often within hours. Diffuse pulmonary capillary leakage causes massive, bilateral pleural effusions and pulmonary edema. Unlike typical septic shock, HCPS causes profound myocardial depression marked by an abnormally low cardiac index and elevated systemic vascular resistance. The lack of targeted drug therapies restricts clinical options purely to supportive care. Aggressive fluid resuscitation to correct hypotension routinely worsens pulmonary edema and hypoxemia due to the underlying capillary leak. Consequently, managing low cardiac output requires early, carefully titrated inotropic therapy rather than massive volume expansion. Extracorporeal membrane oxygenation serves as the primary rescue therapy for refractory shock, but its deployment requires specialized pediatric centers and carries significant risks of severe hemorrhage or limb ischemia. Ultimately, successful management hinges on maintaining a high index of suspicion when history suggests exposure, initiating early and aggressive treatment for shock and respiratory failure, and ensuring rapid transfer to high-acuity pediatric centers. — Jamil A. Abbasi, MD Baylor Scott & White All Saints Medical Center, Fort Worth, Texas, USA jamil.abbasi@bswhealth.org References - 1.Lilitwat W, Mahindrakar N, Bhandari P, et al. Hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome in children: a systematic scoping review of presentation, critical care management, and outcomes. Proc (Bayl Univ Med Cent). 2026;39(6):1118–1127. doi: 10.1080/08998280.2026.2698359. [DOI] [PubMed] [Google Scholar]

papers.title: Prevalence and Genetic Diversity of Zoonotic Leptospira and Hantavirus in Rodents, Lanxi City, 2023-2025.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Leptospirosis (caused by Leptospira, a bacterium) and hantavirus disease (caused by hantavirus, a virus) are important zoonoses with rodents as main reservoirs. In this study, we investigated the prevalence and genetic diversity of Leptospira and hantavirus in rodents from rural Lanxi City, Zhejiang Province. Rodents showed a higher Leptospira carriage rate than the national average. All hantavirus isolates were Seoul virus (SEOV) and displayed high genetic divergence from vaccine strains. Notably, a unique local phylogenetic cluster of Leptospira borgpetersenii was identified, indicating potential vaccine mismatch and local evolutionary divergence. METHODS: Samples were collected from April 2023 to August 2025, with intensive trapping from April to August annually in 2023-2024 and additional sampling in April 2025. Liver and kidney tissues were collected via aseptic dissection. Real-time fluorescent PCR was used to detect pathogen nucleic acids, and gene sequencing and phylogenetic analysis were performed on positive samples. RESULTS: A total of 350 rodents were captured, with Rattus norvegicus (brown rat) as the dominant species (80.00%). The overall Leptospira carriage rate was 7.14% (25/350), with the highest rate in R. norvegicus (7.86%). The overall hantavirus carriage rate was 1.43% (5/350), distributed mainly in R. norvegicus and Rattus flavipectus (yellow-breasted rat). No coinfection with both pathogens was detected. Genetic analysis identified 12 Leptospira strains as Leptospira interrogans and 2 as L. borgpetersenii; the latter showed genetic differences from domestic and foreign strains, suggesting a potential evolutionary trend. The two hantavirus strains were both SEOV, closely related to domestic SEOV strains from 2021 but with only 86.08-86.81% nucleotide homology to vaccine strains (e.g., 80-39, Z37), indicating natural variation. papers.title: The 2026 Andes hantavirus outbreak: a renewed call for global zoonotic preparedness
papers.abstract: The 2026 cluster of Andes virus (ANDV) infection linked to the expedition cruise ship MV Hondius resulted in 13 cases (12 laboratory-confirmed and one probable), including three deaths, and required the monitoring of more than 650 contacts across more than 30 countries and territories before the World Health Organization (WHO) declared the outbreak over on 2 July 2026. Available evidence suggests a single land-based zoonotic exposure before embarkation, followed by limited person-to-person transmission on board. Although WHO assessed the global risk as low throughout, the event exposed recurring weaknesses in zoonotic preparedness, including delayed clinical recognition in a remote setting, maritime outbreak protocols oriented toward other pathogens, and the burden of multinational contact tracing for an infection with an incubation period of up to 6 weeks. This editorial examines these lessons in light of earlier ANDV outbreaks and argues for closer integration of One Health surveillance, maritime health security, and the International Health Regulations in preparing for rare but high-consequence zoonoses.
papers.journal: International Journal of Surgery: Global Health

papers.title: Hantaviruses at the human-animal-environment interface: a One Health review of rodent reservoirs, surveillance, and preparedness
papers.abstract: Hantaviruses maintained in small mammals cause hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome. Exposure usually arises from contact with infected rodent excreta, so prevention depends on understanding reservoir ecology, human activities, and the settings in which they intersect. This structured narrative review synthesizes evidence on host relationships, exposure, clinical and laboratory recognition, genomic investigation, and One Health surveillance across several regions. We propose three risk-proportionate tiers: baseline readiness where evidence is sparse, enhanced investigation after a credible signal, and sustained integrated surveillance where transmission is established. Five shared functions are scaled across tiers: reservoir sampling, clinical recognition and referral testing, molecular characterization, occupational and environmental assessment, and cross-sector data review. Published outbreaks in Croatia and long-running surveillance in Panama illustrate how the decision logic could be applied, while the 2026 Andes virus cruise-ship event highlights the need for diagnostics and contact management. The framework provides a practical way to plan surveillance with limited resources, but its triggers, workload, and impact remain to be evaluated prospectively.

analysis_zh.background: 汉坦病毒es 在小型哺乳动物中导致 肾综合征出血热 和 汉坦病毒心肺综合征。
analysis_zh.main_directions: 暴露源于与受感染啮齿动物排泄物的接触,因此防控关键在于了解储存宿主生态、人类活动以及交叉环境。
analysis_zh.current_state: 本回顾综合了多个地区关于宿主关系、暴露、临床与实验室识别、基因组研究以及 One Health 监测的证据。
analysis_zh.gaps: 所提出的分层框架的触发条件、工作负荷和影响尚未进行前瞻性评估。
analysis_zh.future_research: 实施并前瞻性评估三层风险比例分级,扩大储存宿主抽样、临床识别、分子特征分析、职业风险评估以及跨部门数据审查,以确定其有效性和资源需求。

papers.summary_zh: 背景：汉坦病毒es 在小型哺乳动物中导致 肾综合征出血热 和 汉坦病毒心肺综合征。 主要方向：暴露源于与受感染啮齿动物排泄物的接触,因此防控关键在于了解储存宿主生态、人类活动以及交叉环境。 研究现状：本回顾综合了多个地区关于宿主关系、暴露、临床与实验室识别、基因组研究以及 One Health 监测的证据。 不足：所提出的分层框架的触发条件、工作负荷和影响尚未进行前瞻性评估。 后续研究：实施并前瞻性评估三层风险比例分级,扩大储存宿主抽样、临床识别、分子特征分析、职业风险评估以及跨部门数据审查,以确定其有效性和资源需求。

papers.title: Continent-wide Multi-Segment Phylogenomic Study of Host and Geographic Structuring of African Hantaviruses
papers.abstract: Abstract Background: African hantaviruses remain among the least characterized members of the family Hantaviridae , with fragmented genomic data limiting our understanding of their evolutionary relationships, host associations, and geographic structuring. Here, we investigated the integrated continent-wide phylogenomic structure of African hantaviruses using all three coding genomic segments. Methods: We compiled and curated 281 full-length and partial coding sequences representing the L segment ( n = 166), M segment ( n = 48), and S segment ( n = 67) from 13 African countries, alongside representative global reference strains. Temporal signal was evaluated using root-to-tip regression analysis. Segment-specific phylogenetic reconstructions were performed to characterize host-associated and geographic structuring. Additionally, pairwise tanglegram comparisons of the L, M, and S phylogenies were constructed to evaluate topological congruence and identify potential signals of genetic reassortment. Results Root-to-tip regressions revealed weak temporal signal across the L ( R 2 = 0.069), M ( R 2 = 0.021), and S ( R 2 = 0.046) datasets, precluding reliable molecular-clock inference. Phylogenetic analyses demonstrated pronounced host-associated and geographic structuring across all three segments. Rodent, shrew, and bat-associated hantaviruses formed distinct evolutionary clades, with bat and shrew-borne lineages occupying basal, divergent positions relative to rodent-associated viruses. Keywords: African hantaviruses, Phylogenomics, Orthohantavirus, One Health, Virus-host co-divergence, Zoonotic surveillance Introduction Emerging zoonotic viruses, including hantaviruses, continue to pose significant threats to global public health [1,2]. Africa is recognized as a hotspot for pathogen emergence because of its exceptional biodiversity, rapid environmental change, and increasing human–wildlife interactions [3]. Although considerable attention has focused on high-profile viral haemorrhagic fevers such as Ebola virus disease and Lassa fever, the diversity, ecology, and evolutionary history of many other zoonotic viruses remain poorly understood. Among these neglected pathogens are hantaviruses (family Hantaviridae), which were historically regarded as rodent-borne viruses distributed predominantly across Europe, Asia, and the Americas [1].. However, increasing molecular surveillance over the past two decades has demonstrated that hantaviruses are also widely distributed throughout Africa and circulate in diverse mammalian hosts, revealing substantially broader evolutionary and ecological diversity than previously recognized [4,5]. Members of the family Hantaviridae are enveloped viruses with a tripartite, negative- sense, single-stranded RNA genome comprising the Small (S), Medium (M), and Large (L) segments, which encode the nucleocapsid protein, glycoprotein precursor, and RNA-dependent RNA polymerase, respectively [6]. Hantaviruses were traditionally considered highly host-associated viruses that evolved predominantly in rodents through long-term virus–host associations [7,8]. However, the discovery of genetically divergent hantaviruses in shrews, moles, and bats substantially expanded this paradigm and demonstrated that the evolutionary diversity of the family extends across multiple mammalian orders [5,9]. These discoveries are particularly relevant to Africa, which represents an important but underexplored reservoir of hantavirus diversity, harbouring diverse ecosystems and mammalian hosts that remain incompletely characterized [10,11]. The discovery of Sangassou virus in the African wood mouse (Hylomyscus simus) in Guinea provided the first molecular evidence of an indigenous African rodent- associated hantavirus and established that African rodents harbour evolutionarily distinct viral lineages [6,12]. Subsequent investigations expanded the known diversity through the identification of Tanganya virus and Bowe virus in Crocidura shrews in Guinea [9], Azagny virus in the West African pygmy shrew (Crocidura obscurior) in Côte d'Ivoire [13], and highly divergent hantaviruses in banana pipistrelle bats (Neoromicia nanus) from Côte d'Ivoire [14]. Rodent-, shrew-, and bat-associated hantaviruses have subsequently been reported from Gabon, Sierra Leone, Kenya, Ethiopia, Tanzania, the Democratic Republic of Congo, Madagascar, Egypt, Senegal, Benin, and, more recently, Mali, highlighting the substantial host and geographic diversity of African hantaviruses [15,16,17,18]. The increasing availability of viral genomic sequences has revealed pronounced host- associated and geographic structuring among African hantaviruses [19,20]. Previous phylogenetic investigations indicate that indigenous African hantaviruses comprise several deeply divergent evolutionary lineages associated with rodents, shrews, and bats, whereas Seoul orthohantavirus (SEOV), primarily associated with commensal Rattus species, exhibits broader phylogenetic relationships with globally distributed lineages [17]. These observations suggest that African hantavirus diversity comprises geographically structured endemic lineages alongside widely distributed commensal- rodent-associated viruses. Nevertheless, the evolutionary relationships among these lineages and the extent to which host association and geographic structure are conserved across genomic segments remain incompletely resolved because most previous studies have focused on individual virus species, single genomic segments, or restricted geographic regions. Understanding the evolutionary ecology of African hantaviruses is increasingly important because ecological disturbance, urbanization, agricultural intensification, climate variability, and habitat fragmentation are altering wildlife communities and potentially increasing opportunities for zoonotic spillover [3]. Human infection occurs predominantly through inhalation of aerosolized excreta from infected reservoir hosts, and retrospective serological investigations have provided evidence of human exposure in several African countries [4,6]. However, hantavirus infections remain poorly recognized in routine clinical practice because their nonspecific manifestations overlap with those of malaria, typhoid fever, Lassa fever, leptospirosis, and other endemic febrile illnesses [21]. Consequently, the burden of hantavirus infection in Africa is likely underestimated, particularly in countries such as Nigeria, where hantavirus diversity and human infection remain poorly characterized. The recent 2026 Andes virus outbreak associated with the M/V Hondius cruise ship further demonstrates the potential for hantaviruses to generate cross-border public-health events requiring multinational surveillance, laboratory investigation, contact tracing, and coordinated international responses [22]. These observations emphasize the need to strengthen hantavirus surveillance within broader One Health frameworks for emerging zoonotic disease detection and preparedness. The segmented genome of hantaviruses provides an important basis for investigating whether evolutionary patterns are consistently represented across different genomic regions. Because the L, M, and S segments encode proteins with distinct biological functions, they may experience different evolutionary constraints, rates of sequence change, and selective pressures [23,24]. The L segment encodes the RNA-dependent RNA polymerase and contains relatively conserved regions that can provide phylogenetic information across divergent lineages, whereas the M segment encodes the viral glycoprotein precursor involved in virus–host cell interactions and may exhibit substantial sequence variation among viral lineages. The S segment encodes the nucleocapsid protein and provides an additional functionally distinct marker for resolving evolutionary relationships. Consequently, phylogenies reconstructed from individual genomic segments may differ in their ability to resolve deep and shallow evolutionary relationships, including geographic and host-associated lineages [11,23,24]. In addition, comparison of segment-specific phylogenies enables assessment of whether viral lineages share a common evolutionary history. Strong topological concordance among segment phylogenies supports a broadly shared evolutionary history, whereas phylogenetic incongruence may reflect genetic reassortment or other segment-specific evolutionary processes [25,26]. Reassortment can occur following co-infection of a host with genetically distinct viruses and may generate discordant evolutionary histories among genomic segments [6,26]. Comparative analysis across all three genomic segments is therefore important for distinguishing robust host- and geographic-associated evolutionary patterns from signals specific to individual genomic regions. Despite the increasing discovery of genetically diverse hantaviruses in Africa, a continent-wide comparative framework integrating evolutionary relationships, host associations, geographic structure, and genomic congruence remains limited [11,17,27]. In particular, the extent to which host- and geographic-associated phylogenetic patterns are concordantly recovered across the L, M, and S genomic segments remains poorly characterized at the continental scale. Addressing these gaps is important for understanding the evolutionary organization of African hantavirus diversity and for identifying genomic and ecological priorities for One Health surveillance. In the present study, we performed a continent-wide comparative phylogenomic analysis of African hantaviruses using the L, M, and S genomic segments. We analysed 281 full-length and partial coding sequences from 13 African countries together with representative global reference sequences to characterize host- associated and geographic structuring and assess phylogenetic congruence among genomic segments. Pairwise tanglegram analyses were used to assess topological congruence among the L, M, and S phylogenies and identify discordant relationships potentially consistent with reassortment. By integrating multi-segment phylogenetic evidence with reservoir-host and geographic information, this study establishes a continent-wide framework for understanding the evolutionary structure of African hantaviruses and provides a foundation for future genomic surveillance, One Health preparedness, and global health security. Materials and Methods Sequence dataset A total of 281 hantavirus nucleotide sequences representing the three genomic segments were analyzed: 48 M-segment, 67 S-segment, and 166 L-segment sequences (Supplementary Table 1). All sequences from Africa (Egypt, Senegal, Benin, Mali, Guinea, Côte d'Ivoire, Sierra Leone, Gabon, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Ethiopia, Kenya, Tanzania, and Madagascar) were retrieved from National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI) GenBank and represent isolates collected between 2004 and 2024 with no isolates from 2025 together with selected reference strains from Asia, Europe, and the Americas to provide global phylogenetic context. Sequence alignment Nucleotide sequences for each genomic segment (L, M, and S) were aligned independently using MAFFT v7 [28] with the --auto algorithm and otherwise default parameters. Alignments were inspected and manually edited in AliView v1.01 [29] to ensure positional homology. Ambiguously aligned regions and sites with excessive gaps were removed prior to phylogenetic inference. Phylogenetic inference Maximum-likelihood (ML) phylogenies for each segment were inferred using IQ- TREE v2.1.3 [30]. For each alignment the best-fit nucleotide substitution model was selected by ModelFinder [31] implemented within IQ-TREE. Node support was assessed with 1,000 ultrafast bootstrap replicates [32]. The ML trees files were exported in Newick format with branch lengths in substitutions/site and visualized in interactive Tree Of Life version 7.6 iTOL [33]. Assessment of temporal signal Temporal signal of each segment dataset was evaluated using Clockor2 v1.9.1 [34] (https://clockor2.github.io). ML trees with branch lengths in substitutions/site (Newick format) and sampling dates (from sequence metadata or CSV file) were used as inputs. Root-to-tip regression was performed independently for the L, M, and S datasets. The temporal signal was judged insufficient to support reliable molecular clock dating. Therefore, time-calibrated Bayesian phylogenetic analyses and molecular clock dating were not performed. Comparative phylogenetic analysis and detection of reassortment To ensure consistent taxon labels across segment datasets, isolates were assigned unique identifiers (HTV001–HTV198) and a mapping file linking identifiers to accession numbers and metadata is provided in Supplementary Table 1. Trees were rooted consistently by midpoint rooting in FigTree v1.4.4 [35]. Congruence among the L, M, and S genomic segments, ML trees were compared using Dendroscope v3.5.7 [36]. Pairwise tanglegrams (L–M, L–S, and M–S) were generated using the Tanglegram module; the built-in untangling algorithm was applied to minimize edge crossings while preserving topology. Trees used for tanglegrams were exported in NEXUS format. Putative reassortment events were identified by examining isolates that occupied incongruent phylogenetic positions between paired segment trees. Particular attention was given to taxa that clustered within different evolutionary lineages while maintaining strong branch support in the original phylogenetic analyses. Given that topological discordance may also arise from incomplete phylogenetic resolution, stochastic error, or differences in evolutionary histories among genomic segments, putative reassortment events were interpreted conservatively by integrating tanglegram patterns with branch support, host species, geographic origin, and the broader phylogenetic context. Results Dataset Characteristics We compiled and curated 281 full-length and partial coding sequences representing the three hantavirus genomic segments: L, encoding the RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (n = 166), M, encoding the glycoprotein precursor (n = 48), and S, encoding the nucleocapsid protein (n = 67) (Supplementary Table 1). The dataset comprised sequences from 13 African countries spanning West n= 70, Central n=2, East n=46, and North Africa n= 16 and Madagascar n=91, together with representative global reference strains (supplementary table 1). African sequences were derived from diverse mammalian hosts, including rodents, shrews, and bats, allowing comparative assessment of host-associated and geographic phylogenetic structure. Assessment of Temporal Signal Root-to-tip regression showed weak temporal structure for the L, M and S datasets (R2 = 0.069, 0.021 and 0.046, respectively), indicating insufficient temporal signal for reliable molecular-clock inference. Consequently, time-calibrated phylogenetic and phylogeographic analyses were not undertaken. Subsequent evolutionary comparisons were therefore based on phylogenetic topology, branch support, host association, and geographic distribution rather than divergence-time estimates. full_text_sections.full_text: Continent-wide Multi-Segment Phylogenomic Study of Host and Geographic Structuring of African Hantaviruses Mkpuma Nicodemus National Veterinary Research Institute Oyekan Olumuyiwa National Veterinary Research Institute Igah Lanre National Veterinary Research Institute Uwem Okon Edet Federal University of Technology Adedeji Jeremy Adeyinka National Veterinary Research Institute Meseko Adebajo Clement National Veterinary Research Institute Research Article Keywords: African hantaviruses, Phylogenomics, Orthohantavirus, One Health, Virus-host co-divergence, Zoonotic surveillance Posted Date: October 29th, 2026 DOI: https://doi.org/10.21203/rs.3.rs-11306203/v1 License:   This work is licensed under a Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License. Read Full License Additional Declarations: No competing interests reported. Continent-wide Multi-Segment Phylogenomic Study of Host and Geographic Structuring of African Hantaviruses. 1Mkpuma Nicodemus*, 1Oyekan Olumuyiwa, 1Igah Lanre, 2Uwem Okon Edet, 1Adedeji Jeremy Adeyinka,1Meseko Adebajo Clement Author’s Affiliation 1National Veterinary Research Institute, Vom, Nigeria 2Department of Microbiology, School of Pure and Applied Sciences, Federal University of Technology, Ikot Abasi, Akwa Ibom State, Nigeria *Corresponding author: nicodemusmkpuma@gmail.com Abstract Background: African hantaviruses remain among the least characterized members of the family Hantaviridae, with fragmented genomic data limiting our understanding of their evolutionary relationships, host associations, and geographic structuring. Here, we investigated the integrated continent-wide phylogenomic structure of African hantaviruses using all three coding genomic segments. Methods: We compiled and curated 281 full-length and partial coding sequences representing the L segment (n = 166), M segment (n = 48), and S segment (n = 67) from 13 African countries, alongside representative global reference strains. Temporal signal was evaluated using root-to-tip regression analysis. Segment-specific phylogenetic reconstructions were performed to characterize host-associated and geographic structuring. Additionally, pairwise tanglegram comparisons of the L, M, and S phylogenies were constructed to evaluate topological congruence and identify potential signals of genetic reassortment. Results: Root-to-tip regressions revealed weak temporal signal across the L (R2 = 0.069), M (R2 = 0.021), and S ( R2 = 0.046) datasets, precluding reliable molecular- clock inference. Phylogenetic analyses demonstrated pronounced host-associated and geographic structuring across all three segments. Rodent, shrew, and bat-associated hantaviruses formed distinct evolutionary clades, with bat and shrew-borne lineages occupying basal, divergent positions relative to rodent-associated viruses. Endemic African hantaviruses exhibited marked regional clustering, forming distinct Malagasy, East African, and West African assemblages, whereas Senegalese, Beninese, and Malian sequences clustered within globally distributed, Rattus-associated Seoul orthohantavirus lineages. Comparative analyses highlighted complementary phylogenetic signals: the L segment provided a robust framework for resolving deep evolutionary relationships, the M segment offered clear discrimination among closely related host and geographic groups, and the S segment consistently recovered primary lineage boundaries. Pairwise tanglegrams demonstrated substantial topological concordance among segments highest between L and M with localized incongruences primarily in the L–S comparison restricted to closely related terminal taxa, consistent with but not definitive evidence of reassortment Conclusions: African hantaviruses display strong host-associated and geographic structuring, with major evolutionary relationships broadly conserved across all three genomic segments. These findings provide an integrated continent-wide phylogenomic framework, establishing a foundation for future genomic surveillance, evolutionary studies, and One Health strategies across Africa. Keywords: African hantaviruses, Phylogenomics, Orthohantavirus, One Health, Virus-host co-divergence, Zoonotic surveillance Introduction Emerging zoonotic viruses, including hantaviruses, continue to pose significant threats to global public health [1,2]. Africa is recognized as a hotspot for pathogen emergence because of its exceptional biodiversity, rapid environmental change, and increasing human–wildlife interactions [3]. Although considerable attention has focused on high-profile viral haemorrhagic fevers such as Ebola virus disease and Lassa fever, the diversity, ecology, and evolutionary history of many other zoonotic viruses remain poorly understood. Among these neglected pathogens are hantaviruses (family Hantaviridae), which were historically regarded as rodent-borne viruses distributed predominantly across Europe, Asia, and the Americas [1].. However, increasing molecular surveillance over the past two decades has demonstrated that hantaviruses are also widely distributed throughout Africa and circulate in diverse mammalian hosts, revealing substantially broader evolutionary and ecological diversity than previously recognized [4,5]. Members of the family Hantaviridae are enveloped viruses with a tripartite, negative- sense, single-stranded RNA genome comprising the Small (S), Medium (M), and Large (L) segments, which encode the nucleocapsid protein, glycoprotein precursor, and RNA-dependent RNA polymerase, respectively [6]. Hantaviruses were traditionally considered highly host-associated viruses that evolved predominantly in rodents through long-term virus–host associations [7,8]. However, the discovery of genetically divergent hantaviruses in shrews, moles, and bats substantially expanded this paradigm and demonstrated that the evolutionary diversity of the family extends across multiple mammalian orders [5,9]. These discoveries are particularly relevant to Africa, which represents an important but underexplored reservoir of hantavirus diversity, harbouring diverse ecosystems and mammalian hosts that remain incompletely characterized [10,11]. The discovery of Sangassou virus in the African wood mouse (Hylomyscus simus) in Guinea provided the first molecular evidence of an indigenous African rodent- associated hantavirus and established that African rodents harbour evolutionarily distinct viral lineages [6,12]. Subsequent investigations expanded the known diversity through the identification of Tanganya virus and Bowe virus in Crocidura shrews in Guinea [9], Azagny virus in the West African pygmy shrew (Crocidura obscurior) in Côte d'Ivoire [13], and highly divergent hantaviruses in banana pipistrelle bats (Neoromicia nanus) from Côte d'Ivoire [14]. Rodent-, shrew-, and bat-associated hantaviruses have subsequently been reported from Gabon, Sierra Leone, Kenya, Ethiopia, Tanzania, the Democratic Republic of Congo, Madagascar, Egypt, Senegal, Benin, and, more recently, Mali, highlighting the substantial host and geographic diversity of African hantaviruses [15,16,17,18]. The increasing availability of viral genomic sequences has revealed pronounced host- associated and geographic structuring among African hantaviruses [19,20]. Previous phylogenetic investigations indicate that indigenous African hantaviruses comprise several deeply divergent evolutionary lineages associated with rodents, shrews, and bats, whereas Seoul orthohantavirus (SEOV), primarily associated with commensal Rattus species, exhibits broader phylogenetic relationships with globally distributed lineages [17]. These observations suggest that African hantavirus diversity comprises geographically structured endemic lineages alongside widely distributed commensal- rodent-associated viruses. papers.title: Predictive Surveillance for Andes Virus Transmission in the Americas.
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT. The 2026 Andes virus outbreak linked to the M/V Hondius cruise ship exposed limitations in conventional, case-based surveillance for zoonotic threats with potential person-to-person transmission. In the present opinion and analysis article, the authors argue that predictive surveillance, supported by artificial intelligence, ecological modeling, and the One Health approach, can strengthen preparedness for hantavirus transmission in the Americas. Current evidence suggests that selected models that incorporate epidemiological, climatic, environmental, and rodent-related variables may provide an anticipatory window of 2 to 12 months, depending on context and data inputs. However, implementation requires more than technical capacity. It depends on interoperable multisectoral data, transparent model governance, local validation, sustainable financing, and technology transfer to avoid widening inequities between health systems. Predictive surveillance should complement conventional surveillance by supporting risk communication, rodent monitoring, laboratory preparedness, and targeted public health action in areas where ecological and epidemiological signals converge.
papers.journal: The American journal of tropical medicine and hygiene

It depends on interoperable multisectoral data, transparent model governance, local validation, sustainable financing, and technology transfer to avoid widening inequities between health systems. Predictive surveillance should complement conventional surveillance by supporting risk communication, rodent monitoring, laboratory preparedness, and targeted public health action in areas where ecological and epidemiological signals converge. papers.title: Anthropogenic drivers of recent ebola and hantavirus outbreaks: A one health perspective
papers.abstract: Recent outbreaks of Ebola Virus Disease (EVD) and hantavirus infection have redrawn attention to the role of anthropogenic environmental change in the emergence of zoonotic diseases. Human activities, including deforestation, agricultural expansion, land-use modification and ecosystem degradation, have increasingly disrupted the interactions between wildlife reservoirs, domestic animals and humans, creating favourable conditions for pathogen spillover. In this commentary, we examine evidence linking these environmental drivers to the emergence and transmission of Ebola virus and hantaviruses, with particular emphasis on the effects of habitat alteration on wildlife ecology, viral evolution and host-pathogen interactions. We further discuss predictive models suggesting that, under current environmental and socioeconomic trajectories, the geographical risk of EVD will continue to expand. These observations underscore the urgent need to move beyond reactive outbreak response towards prevention by addressing the environmental determinants of disease emergence. We argue that the One Health framework, integrating human, animal and environmental health through coordinated multisectoral action, provides the most appropriate strategy for reducing the risk of future zoonotic outbreaks and strengthening global health security.

papers.full_text: Anthropogenic drivers of recent ebola and hantavirus outbreaks: A one health perspective Zacharias Raptopoulos 1 Aristos Aristodimou 2 1 Family Medicine Department, Limassol General Hospital, State Health Organization Services, Limassol, Cyprus 2 Internal Medicine Department, Limassol General Hospital, State Health Organization Services, Limassol, Cyprus Abstract Recent outbreaks of Ebola Virus Disease (EVD) and hantavirus infection have redrawn attention to the role of anthropogenic environmental change in the emergence of zoonotic diseases. Human activities, including deforestation, agricultural expansion, land-use modification and ecosystem degradation, have increasingly disrupted the interactions between wildlife reservoirs, domestic animals and humans, creating favourable conditions for pathogen spillover. In this commentary, we examine evidence linking these environmental drivers to the emergence and transmission of Ebola virus and hantaviruses, with particular emphasis on the effects of habitat alteration on wildlife ecology, viral evolution and host-pathogen interactions. We further discuss predictive models suggesting that, under current environmental and socioeconomic trajectories, the geographical risk of EVD will continue to expand. These observations underscore the urgent need to move beyond reactive outbreak response towards prevention by addressing the environmental determinants of disease emergence. We argue that the One Health framework, integrating human, animal and environmental health through coordinated multisectoral action, provides the most appropriate strategy for reducing the risk of future zoonotic outbreaks and strengthening global health security. Keywords ebola virus, hantavirus infections, ecosystem, global health, human activities, one-health-approach Graphical abstract Introduction Recent outbreaks of Ebola virus and hantavirus infections, occurring against the backdrop of accelerating anthropogenic environmental change, have renewed interest in the role of human activities in the emergence and persistence of zoonotic diseases [1], [2], [3]. Human-driven environmental changes, including climate change, land-use modification, deforestation, urbanization, and ecosystem degradation, have altered the interactions among humans, animals, and the environment, influencing the ecology and geographic distribution of infectious diseases [4], [5], [6], [7], [8], [9]. While outbreak-specific evidence for the most recent Ebola epidemic remains limited, studies of previous outbreaks caused by Zaire Ebola virus have consistently identified recurring anthropogenic and environmental factors—including population expansion, forest encroachment, climate variability, and deficiencies in water and sanitation infrastructure—that may facilitate zoonotic spillover and subsequent disease transmission [10]. Likewise, anthropogenic land-use change and agricultural expansion have been associated with an increased risk of human hantavirus infection through their effects on reservoir host ecology and opportunities for human exposure [11]. Collectively, these observations support the application of the One Health framework, which recognizes the interconnectedness of human, animal, and environmental health. Endorsed by international organizations such as the World Health Organization (WHO), the One Health approach provides a valuable framework for understanding the emergence and spread of zoonotic pathogens, including Ebola virus and hantaviruses [12]. In this commentary, we examine the potential contribution of anthropogenic environmental change to the recent Ebola virus and hantavirus outbreaks through the lens of One Health, drawing upon evidence from previous outbreaks and established ecological principles to discuss mechanisms that may underlie contemporary zoonotic emergence. Anthropogenic drivers of Ebola and hantavirus outbreaks Ebola virus disease (EVD) is caused by one of four pathogenic Ebolavirus species—Zaire, Sudan, Taï Forest and Bundibugyo—all associated with high case-fatality rates [13]. Although definitive reservoir identification remains elusive, Old World fruit bats are considered the most likely natural reservoirs or amplifying hosts [13]. Human infections typically result from zoonotic spillover following encroachment into forested habitats or contact with infected bushmeat [14]. Banik and Basu further argue that intensive farming facilitates viral mutation and reassortment, producing highly infective strains capable of efficient human-to-human transmission [14]. Moreover, approximately 31% of emerging zoonotic diseases, including Ebola virus disease, Nipah virus infection and severe acute respiratory syndrome (SARS), have been associated with land-use change driven by a 300% increase in agricultural expansion over the past 50 years [14]. Additional statistical modelling demonstrated that the probability of Ebola virus spillover in West and Central Africa increases significantly with deforestation, with every 5–10% reduction in forest cover approximately doubling the risk of outbreak occurrence [13], [14]. Hantavirus infection represents another important example of an environmentally driven zoonosis. The virus is maintained in asymptomatic rodent reservoirs and is transmitted to humans primarily through inhalation of aerosolized viral particles from contaminated rodent excreta [15]. Several studies have shown that deforestation and land-use intensification alter reservoir ecology and increase the prevalence of hantavirus infection [15]. Prist et al. describe the “dilution effect”, whereby reductions in non-reservoir species increase the relative abundance of competent reservoir hosts, thereby facilitating viral transmission [15]. Ecosystem-altering human activities not only increase opportunities for viral replication and transmission but may also influence hantavirus evolution. Holmes and Zhang argued that repeated host-switching events, rather than strict virus–host co-divergence, have been a major force shaping hantavirus evolution [16]. Habitat disturbance may further facilitate these evolutionary processes by increasing contact among reservoir species and creating greater opportunities for cross-species transmission [15]. Collectively, these examples demonstrate that anthropogenic environmental change not only increases opportunities for zoonotic spillover but also reshapes host–pathogen interactions, highlighting the need for integrated One Health strategies that address environmental degradation alongside infectious disease surveillance and preparedness. The One Health framework for preventing zoonotic disease emergence Both, EVD and hantavirus infection, have a major impact on human health and society. In addition to their high morbidity and mortality, these zoonoses impose a substantial economic burden on healthcare systems and public health infrastructure [14], [17]. Redding et al. estimated that, under current trajectories of environmental and socioeconomic change, the incidence of EVD will continue to increase [13]. More specifically, the authors predicted that by 2070 the maximum geographical area affected by EVD could expand from 3.45 million km2 to 3.80 million km2 [13]. These projections emphasize that, unless the underlying anthropogenic drivers of disease emergence are addressed, the burden of zoonotic diseases is likely to escalate in the coming decades. The era in which emerging infectious diseases could be managed solely through clinical and public health interventions has long passed. The One Health framework, endorsed by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), recognizes the intrinsic interdependence of human, animal and environmental health and advocates an integrated, collaborative, multisectoral and transdisciplinary approach at the local, regional, national and global levels to prevent future zoonotic outbreaks [14], [17]. Importantly, responsibility for preventing emerging zoonoses should not rest exclusively with Ministries of Health but should be shared across the environmental, forestry and agricultural sectors [18]. Given the strong association between land-use change and zoonotic disease emergence, environmental policies should be regarded as an integral component of infectious disease prevention [14], [18]. Incorporating zoonotic disease risk into environmental impact assessments before large-scale deforestation, agricultural expansion or other ecosystem-altering activities could facilitate the identification of high-risk practices and inform mitigation strategies [18]. Likewise, strengthening surveillance programmes targeting wildlife reservoirs, particularly bats and rodents, together with advances in genomic surveillance, would improve the early detection of pathogens with zoonotic potential before widespread human transmission occurs [18]. Such proactive measures would shift the focus from responding to outbreaks toward preventing them by addressing their underlying anthropogenic drivers. As the recent Ebola and hantavirus outbreaks clearly demonstrate, the prevention of future pandemics depends not only on advances in medicine but also on the protection and sustainable management of the ecosystems upon which human health ultimately depends. Conclusion The recent Ebola Virus Disease and hantavirus outbreaks provide compelling evidence that anthropogenic environmental change is no longer a peripheral contributor to zoonotic disease emergence but one of its principal drivers. Deforestation, agricultural expansion and unsustainable land-use practices continue to reshape ecosystems, increase contact between humans and wildlife reservoirs, and facilitate pathogen spillover with potentially devastating public health consequences. As climate change and environmental degradation intensify, similar outbreaks are likely to become more frequent unless these upstream drivers are addressed. Future preparedness must therefore extend beyond improvements in diagnostics, therapeutics and outbreak surveillance to include policies that protect ecosystems, promote sustainable land management and integrate zoonotic disease risk into environmental decision-making. The One Health approach offers a scientifically grounded framework through which governments, public health authorities, environmental agencies and agricultural sectors can work collaboratively to mitigate the root causes of emerging infectious diseases. Ultimately, preventing the next pandemic will depend not only on advances in medicine but also on our ability to recognize that safeguarding environmental integrity is inseparable from protecting human health. The question is no longer whether anthropogenic environmental change influences the emergence of zoonotic diseases, but whether global health policy will evolve rapidly enough to address these environmental drivers before the next pandemic emerges.
